proxy_language: Proto-Bantu (reconstructed, with Swahili and Zulu as attested Bantu models); Nilotic cattle-herding vocabulary as a secondary layer
proxy_rationale: The label 'Rift-and-Cattle Court' evokes later East/southern African pastoralist-agricultural states (e.g. Great Lakes kingdoms such as Buganda, Bunyoro and Nkore, Great Zimbabwe-era Shona courts, Nguni and Sotho chiefdoms) where cattle are central to wealth and kingship. No single attested language fits, so Bantu is the most defensible family: Proto-Bantu reconstructions (Meeussen 1967, Bantu Lexical Reconstructions) plus well-documented living languages (Swahili, Zulu, Shona, Luganda) supply real morphology. The link to any specific court is weak, hence low confidence.
phonology: Typical Bantu 5-vowel system /a e i o u/ (some languages have 7; Proto-Bantu had 7: *i *e *a *o *u plus *\u1ecb *\u0169 super-high vowels). Consonants: voiceless stops p t k, voiced b d g (many languages), prenasalised stops mb nd ng, nj, nasals m n ny ng', fricatives f v s z sh h, affricates ch j, liquids l (r), glides w y. Click consonants (c q x) only in Nguni/Southern Bantu contact zones. Many languages have tone (not marked in ordinary orthography); Swahili has penultimate stress.
phonotactics: Strictly open syllables (C)V; no consonant clusters other than prenasalised stop units (NC) and C+glide (Cw, Cy, e.g. kwa, mbwa, nya). Words end in a vowel. Syllable shapes: V, CV, NCV, CGV. Nasal syllabic m/n possible before another consonant at morpheme edge (mtu, mbuzi). Vowel hiatus is common (kuona, ua); vowel sequences often resolve by glide formation (w/y). Stress usually penultimate; tone not written.
orthography: Standard Bantu Latin practice (Swahili/Zulu/Shona style): a e i o u; b ch d dh f g h j k l m n ng ng' ny p r s sh t th v w y z; prenasalised mb nd ng nj nz mv. Reconstructed Proto-Bantu forms written with asterisk and Meeussen notation (e.g. *-n\u0254\u0301ng\u0254, *-g\u0254\u0301mb\u025b), but game names should be plain attested-style Latin forms. Noun-class prefix is written attached to the root (mtu, watu, ngombe, kiti).
morphology: Agglutinative; nouns consist of noun-class prefix + root (Proto-Bantu classes 1/2 mu-/ba- persons, 3/4 mu-/mi- trees and things, 5/6 di-/ma- augmentative and masses, 7/8 ki-/bi- (Swahili ki-/vi-) tools and diminutives, 9/10 N-/N- animals and loans, 11 lu-/u-, 12 ka-/tu- diminutive, 14 bu-/u- abstracts, 15 ku- infinitives, 16-18 locatives pa- ku- mu-). Verbs: subject prefix + tense + root + extensions (-ik- stative, -ish- causative, -an- reciprocal, -w- passive) + final vowel -a. Agent nouns: mu-/wa- + verb stem + -i or -a (mfanyi, muvuvi). Places are formed with locative suffix -ni (Swahili) or prefix + stem. Reduplication marks intensity or diminutive.
compounding: True compounding is limited; instead, relations are expressed with associative (genitive) constructions: head noun + associative marker -a- with class agreement (class 7 cha, class 9 ya, class 1 wa, class 5 la, class 3 wa, class 6 ya, class 8 vya, class 11 wa, class 14 wa, class 15 kwa) + possessor noun. 'X of Y' = X + agreeing -a + Y (kiti cha mfalme 'throne of the king'). 'Y-maker' = mu- + verb stem + -i, or mu- + noun for the practitioner (mchungaji 'herder'). Descriptive names put the head first, followed by qualifiers.
noun_phrase_order: Head-initial: Noun + associative phrase / possessive / adjective / demonstrative (kiti kikubwa 'big chair'; ng'ombe wa mfalme 'cattle of the king'). Adjectives and possessives agree with the noun class via concord prefix. Numerals and demonstratives follow the noun.

notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. Proxy is a broad Bantu pastiche; the real courts in this region spoke many unrelated languages (Nilotic, Cushitic, Bantu), so avoid claiming any specific attested court language. Keep to open syllables, vowel-final words, class-prefix + root structure, and head-initial associative phrases with correct concord (ya/cha/wa/za). A trailing vowel check is the simplest audit: every word must end in a vowel; an apostrophe is only legitimate in ng'. Several roots above are Swahili with Arabic or Bantu-internal origins; they are attested words, but only marked reconstructed where an asterisk form is given. The final root entry is a loose model of a Proto-Bantu shape rather than a firm reconstruction and should be treated cautiously.
